Overview

Two days after launching Tay, a chatbot for 18- to 24-year-olds in the US, on Twitter, Microsoft apologises for its offensive tweets and explains that Tay is offline. Tay followed XiaoIce, a chatbot used by some 40 million people in China, and was meant to test whether such an AI would be as engaging in a very different culture. Microsoft says it built a lot of filtering, ran user studies with diverse groups and stress-tested Tay before inviting a wider audience, expecting the AI to improve through interaction. Within the first 24 hours, a coordinated attack by a subset of users "exploited a vulnerability in Tay", and Tay tweeted grossly offensive words and images. Microsoft calls this a critical oversight for this specific attack, takes full responsibility, and says it is fixing the vulnerability and will bring Tay back only when it can better anticipate malicious intent. The closing lesson is that AI systems feed off both positive and negative interactions, so the challenges are as much social as technical, and that doing AI right requires iterating in public, with caution.

Limits

  • The vulnerability is never named. The post does not say what was exploited, how, or whether Tay's model was changed by the abuse; it mentions no "repeat after me" feature and no learning mechanism beyond expecting the AI to get better through interaction.
  • An apology, not a post-mortem. It gives no timeline beyond "the first 24 hours", no numbers and no description of the fix.
  • A live page. The digest covers today's HTML, which wraps the 2016 text in current site navigation, so it will not match a capture from another day.
